ch35.title: New Religious Movements
ch35.summary: The explosion of brand-new religions in the last two centuries — from Joseph Smith's golden plates to the global movements of today. The neutral term that replaced 'cult'; the millenarian ferment of 19th-century America (the Latter-day Saints, Adventists, Jehovah's Witnesses, Christian Science); the global 20th century (Baha'i, Scientology, Falun Gong, Hare Krishna) and its tragedies (Jonestown); the 'cult' question judged by conduct not novelty; and a symbology of new scriptures and staged initiation — taking each movement seriously as religion while keeping a clear eye on harm.
ch35.plateCaption: A new scripture beneath a rising star — the fresh revelations and founders’ books of the modern religions. An original emblem for the phenomenon, not any one movement.

ch36.title: Spiritualism
ch36.summary: The religion of the talking dead — born from two girls and a knocking sound in 1848, swept through a grieving Victorian world of darkened parlors and rapping tables. The Fox sisters and their 1888 confession; the séance and its wonders (rapping, table-tipping, automatic writing, spirit photography, the Ouija board); the appeal to a war-bereaved age and to women; the exposures and the Society for Psychical Research; and a symbology of the coded rap and the 'spiritual telegraph' — keeping the real consolation distinct from the never-verified communication.

ch36.plateCaption: A planchette — the pointer of the talking board, through which the séance spelled its messages letter by letter. An original geometric rendering, not a specific board.

ch37.title: Theosophy & the Occult Revival
ch37.summary: The late-19th-century rebirth of Western esotericism — a claimed ancient wisdom behind all religions, hidden Masters, and a magical order that fused Kabbalah and tarot into a system of the soul. Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, the Secret Doctrine and the root races, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, Crowley's Thelema, and Steiner; a symbology section on the tarot mapped onto the Tree of Life and the Hermetic 'as above, so below' — reckoning honestly with the fraudulent Mahatma letters, the invented pedigrees, and the dark later misuse of the root-race doctrine.
ch37.plate: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="plate-art" viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="84" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="255 20"/><path d="M100 12 l6 -8 l-12 0 z" fill="#e7c680"/><g stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.2"><path d="M100 50 L142 122 L58 122 Z"/><path d="M100 150 L142 78 L58 78 Z"/></g><g stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.6"><circle cx="100" cy="92" r="9"/><line x1="100" y1="101" x2="100" y2="126"/><line x1="88" y1="112" x2="112" y2="112"/></g></svg>
ch37.plateCaption: A synthesis emblem — the ouroboros of eternity, the interlaced triangles of “as above, so below,” and the ankh of life — in the manner of Theosophy’s joining of all sacred signs. An original composite, not a facsimile of any seal.

ch38.title: Wicca & Modern Paganism
ch38.summary: The 20th-century rebirth of Pagan religion — a nature faith of Goddess and Horned God, coven and sabbat, magic and moon. Gerald Gardner and the (false) claim of an ancient surviving witch-cult; the honest origins in ceremonial magic, Romanticism, and folk custom; the Wheel of the Year and the Wiccan Rede; the wider revival (Druidry, Heathenry, the Goddess movement); and a symbology of the pentacle and the Book of Shadows — told as a real, living modern religion that need not be old to be genuine.
ch38.plate: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="plate-art" viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="92" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.3"/><g stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.4"><circle cx="100" cy="40" r="11"/><path d="M84 30 A 14 14 0 0 0 84 50"/><path d="M116 30 A 14 14 0 0 1 116 50"/></g><circle cx="100" cy="118" r="52" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M100 68 L135 176 L44 109 L156 109 L65 176 Z" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/></svg>
ch38.plateCaption: The pentacle — the five-pointed star of the four elements crowned by spirit, bound in the circle of unity — beneath the triple moon of the Goddess. An original geometric rendering of the Wiccan emblem.

ch39.title: Satanism
ch39.summary: Two completely different things wearing the same frightening name: the imaginary Devil-cult that persecutors invent (the witch trials, the blood-libel, the 1980s Satanic Panic — investigated and found baseless) and the real, mostly atheistic philosophy people actually choose. LaVey's Church of Satan and the Satanic Bible (Satan as symbol, not deity), The Satanic Temple's non-theistic church-state activism, and the small theistic fringe; a symbology of the inverted pentagram, Lévi's Baphomet, and the largely-literary Black Mass — described with the same rigor as any tradition and none of the shock.
ch39.plate: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="plate-art" viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="92" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.3"/><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="66" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M100 160 L135 51 L43 119 L157 119 L65 51 Z" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linejoin="round"/></svg>
ch39.plateCaption: The inverted pentagram — the symbol modern self-identified Satanists reclaim as an emblem of the carnal and the self, spirit turned toward matter. An original geometric rendering; a reclaimed sign, described, not endorsed.

ch40.title: African Diaspora Religions
ch40.summary: The living Afro-Atlantic faiths that grew from the African religions carried into slavery — Haitian Vodou, Cuban Santería, Brazilian Candomblé, and the newer fire of Rastafari. From the oath at Bois Caïman and the Haitian Revolution, through the lwa and orichas doubled behind Catholic saints, possession and drumming, to Haile Selassie, Babylon and Zion; a symbology of the vèvè, the bead-codes, the calling drums, and concealment itself — seeing them as the rich, healing, community faiths they are, behind the racist 'voodoo' caricature. Completes the story begun in African Traditional Religion and closes the Modern age.
ch40.plateCaption: A vèvè-style crossroads — the sign of the gatekeeper who must open the way before any spirit can be reached, the ground-drawn sigils at the heart of Vodou and its kin. An original rendering in the tradition’s idiom, not a specific vèvè.

ch64.title: Pentecostalism & Global Christianity
ch64.summary: The fire and the southern shift — the fastest-growing movement in modern religion, and the transformation of Christianity into a Global-South faith. The Azusa Street Revival (1906) under William Seymour and the Holiness roots (Parham, 1901); the baptism in the Holy Spirit and the restored gifts — speaking in tongues, prophecy, and divine healing, modeled on Acts 2; the three waves (classical Pentecostal denominations, the 1960s Charismatic movement into the mainline and Catholic churches, and the neo-charismatic independents); the prosperity gospel, reported honestly and contested; and the demographic shift of the Christian majority to Africa, Latin America, and Asia. A symbology of the tongues of fire, the raised hands, and the laying on of hands — an aniconic Christianity of direct experience, with its theological claims marked as faith.
ch64.plateCaption: Tongues of fire, from the Pentecost story of Acts 2, above two raised open hands, the posture of Pentecostal and charismatic worship. The movement uses few images; this is an original, interpretive drawing.

ch65.title: Bahá'í & New Faiths
ch65.summary: One God, one religion, one humanity — the archive’s closing chapter, on the faith that tries to hold all the others in a single embrace. The Bahá'í Faith: the Báb (executed 1850) and Bahá'u’lláh (1817–1892), exiled to ʾAkká; the three onenesses and the doctrine of progressive revelation, which gathers Abraham, Krishna, Moses, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Báb, and Bahá'u’lláh into one unfolding succession of Manifestations; the strikingly modern social teachings (equality of the sexes, harmony of science and religion, world peace); a clergy-less order under the Universal House of Justice in Haifa; and the systematic persecution of Bahá’ís in Iran. Plus the wider modern ‘new world faiths’ — Caodaism, the Ahmadiyya, Tenrikyo. A symbology of the nine-pointed star, the Greatest Name, and the terraced mountain — with progressive revelation flagged as the faith’s own framework, not neutral history.
ch65.plateCaption: The nine-pointed star, used by Bahá’ís as a symbol of completeness and unity, nine being the highest single digit. An original rendering.

v75.title: The Golden Plates
v75.dated: Obtained, by Joseph Smith's account, on 22 September 1827
v75.held: Not held: Joseph Smith said he returned them to the angel Moroni. The manuscripts of the Book of Mormon are held by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
v75.summary: Metal plates engraved in 'reformed Egyptian' that Joseph Smith said an angel led him to in a hill in western New York, and from which he dictated the Book of Mormon, published in 1830. Eleven witnesses signed statements that they had seen them. No one else has, and their existence and nature are matters of faith and debate.

v73.title: The Book of the Law
v73.dated: Written in Cairo on 8, 9 and 10 April 1904
v73.held: The handwritten manuscript survives in private hands; facsimiles have been published since 1938
v73.summary: Sixty-five handwritten pages that Aleister Crowley said were dictated to him in a Cairo hotel in April 1904 by a being called Aiwass, and the scripture of his religion, Thelema: 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law.' The manuscript was lost and found again five years later in his attic, behind a pair of skis.

v01.title: The Voynich Manuscript
v01.held: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University — MS 408
v01.summary: A fifteenth-century vellum book in an unknown script that no one has been able to read — radiocarbon-dated, its owners traced from Rudolf II's Prague, and every proposed 'solution' tested and found wanting. Study all of Yale's page scans at full resolution, load the standard transliteration, and test a decipherment of your own.

v03.title: The Emerald Tablet
v03.held: No physical tablet is known — the text survives in Arabic & Latin sources
v03.summary: Fourteen lines that became the scripture of European alchemy — 'that which is below is like that which is above.' Traced from the Arabic Book of the Secret of Creation to Newton's own translation, with the Latin and a line-by-line working translation, and kept apart from Doreal's 20th-century 'Tablets of Thoth.'

v19.title: The Book of Soyga
v19.held: Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Bodley 908); British Library (Sloane MS 8)
v19.summary: John Dee's book of magic, ending in 36 grids of letters he could never read. An angel told him only Michael could explain it. Rediscovered in 1994; in 2006 a cryptographer showed the grids are generated from seed words by a fixed rule, not hidden messages.

v85.title: The Picatrix
v85.dated: Arabic original, al-Andalus, 10th–11th century; Castilian translation 1256–1258
v85.held: Arabic, Castilian-derived Latin and vernacular manuscripts in many libraries
v85.summary: The Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm, 'The Goal of the Sage', an Arabic handbook of astral magic from Muslim Spain, translated for Alfonso X and known in Latin as Picatrix. It teaches how to make talismans at the right celestial moment. Its authorship is disputed.

v72.title: The Book of Shadows
v72.dated: Begun c. 1946–1949 as 'Ye Bok of ye Art Magical'; revised through the 1950s
v72.held: Gerald Gardner's own manuscripts in private hands; copied by hand by generations of initiates
v72.summary: The handwritten ritual book of Gerald Gardner's witchcraft, copied by each new initiate, and the founding scripture of Wicca. Gardner presented its rites as those of a surviving ancient witch cult; historians have traced them to twentieth-century sources, from Crowley to folklore, and to Doreen Valiente's poetry.

v74.title: The Satanic Bible
v74.held: Published by Avon Books, New York, 1969; in print ever since
v74.summary: Anton LaVey's book of 1969, the founding text of the Church of Satan: an atheist philosophy of self-interest, indulgence and personal responsibility, in which Satan is a symbol, not a being. It borrows heavily from an 1896 tract and from John Dee's Enochian calls, and it remains in print.

v77.title: The Haitian Vèvè
v77.dated: A living practice; documented from the 19th and 20th centuries
v77.held: Drawn anew for each ceremony and effaced during it; recorded in published collections such as Milo Rigaud's Vè-Vè (1974)
v77.summary: Designs traced on the temple floor in cornmeal, flour or ash by a Vodou priest or priestess to call a particular lwa, or spirit: a cross and cane for Legba, serpents for Damballa, a heart for Ezili. Each is made to be danced over and erased. Their origins in Kongo and Fon sign-traditions are still being traced.

v66.title: The Kebra Nagast
v66.dated: Compiled c. 1314–1322 CE; surviving manuscripts mostly later
v66.held: Many Ge'ez manuscripts in Ethiopia and in European libraries (British Library's Magdala collection among them)
v66.summary: Ethiopia's 'Glory of the Kings': how the Queen of Sheba visited Solomon, bore his son Menelik, and how Menelik brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. It gave the Solomonic dynasty its legitimacy for 650 years, and it is revered by Rastafari. A copy looted from Magdala was returned to Ethiopia in 1872.

v76.title: The Báb's Star Tablet
v76.dated: Written between 1844 and 1850, the years of the Báb's mission
v76.held: British Library, London (Or. 6887), among other star tablets of the Báb
v76.summary: A tablet in the Báb's own hand, its lines of Arabic writing laid out as a five-pointed star, the haykal or 'temple', whose points stand for the head, hands and feet of the human body. The Báb, the forerunner of the Bahá'í Faith, wrote such stars as talismans, full of letter-numbers and derivatives of the word Bahá, 'glory'.
v76.noImage: The Vault shows no image connected with the Báb, out of respect for Bahá'í practice.

baphomet.name: Baphomet
baphomet.desc: Named in the 1307–1312 trials of the Knights Templar as an idol they supposedly worshipped. The familiar winged, goat-headed image was drawn by Éliphas Lévi in 1856 and later adopted by modern Satanism.
baphomet.contested: The Templar confessions were extracted under torture, and historians do not accept that they worshipped any such idol.

horned-god.name: The Horned God
horned-god.desc: The god of modern Wicca, lord of animals, the hunt and death, partner of the Goddess.
horned-god.contested: His form was shaped by Margaret Murray's theory of a surviving pagan witch cult, which historians now reject.

triple-goddess.name: The Triple Goddess
triple-goddess.desc: The Goddess of modern Wicca and Paganism in threefold form, popularised by Robert Graves in The White Goddess (1948).
triple-goddess.contested: Ancient triple goddesses existed, but the idea of one universal Triple Goddess is modern.

satan.name: Satan
satan.desc: In the Hebrew Bible 'the satan' is an accuser in God's court (Job); later Jewish and Christian writings make him the chief enemy of God. Modern Satanists use him as a symbol of rebellion.

papa-legba.name: Papa Legba
papa-legba.desc: The Vodou lwa who opens the gate between people and the spirits and is saluted first in every ceremony; he is related to Legba and Eshu of West Africa.

obatala.name: Ọbàtálá
obatala.desc: Orisha who shaped human bodies from clay, associated with purity, calm judgement and the colour white.

ogun.name: Ògún
ogun.desc: Orisha of iron, hunting, war and technology, patron of smiths, drivers and everyone who works with metal.

shango.name: Ṣàngó
shango.desc: Orisha of thunder and lightning, remembered as a king of Oyo, whose emblem is the double axe.

oshun.name: Ọ̀ṣun
oshun.desc: Orisha of the Osun river, of love, fertility and sweet water, honoured each year at the sacred grove of Osogbo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

eshu.name: Èṣù
eshu.desc: Messenger between people and the orishas and keeper of the crossroads, who must be honoured first. Missionaries wrongly equated him with the Devil.

yemoja.name: Yemọja
yemoja.desc: Orisha of the Ogun river and, in the Americas as Yemayá, of the ocean; a mother of the orishas.
